# Working in this repo

Switchboard is a macOS desktop app (Rust, egui/eframe 0.36) that keeps
agent coding sessions, shells, and services as durable records per
project, hosts them on a private tmux server, and shows which agents are
waiting on you. The idea in one line: **workspaces are data, processes are
a cache.** Every feature asks "what is the on-disk record and how is it
rehydrated?" before "what does the pane look like?"

## Where to read first

- `docs/design.md` is the spec. "Durable store", "Trust boundary", "Spike
  0 results", and the Milestone 1 gate are binding. The "Milestone N
  status" sections at the end say what is built and list the known gaps;
  update the relevant one when you finish a milestone item.
- `README.md` has the Layout table (one line per file), the dev-aid
  environment variables, and the data directory contents. Keep all three
  current.
- `spikes/*/README.md` hold verified commands and measured numbers. Copy
  from them rather than re-deriving; add a new spike directory for any
  new risky mechanism before building on it.
- `docs/lessons.md` explains why the architecture is shaped this way.
- `vendor/egui_term/SWITCHBOARD-PATCHES.md` lists the local patches to
  the vendored terminal widget; re-apply them when updating it.

## Commands

```sh
cargo test --locked --workspace                      # unit + headless UI + tmux tests, every crate
cargo test --locked -p egui_term --lib               # the vendored terminal widget (outside the workspace)
cargo clippy --locked --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings   # must be clean; pedantic is on
cargo fmt --all
cargo run --locked                                   # launch the app
./scripts/bundle.sh                                  # ~/Applications/Switchboard.app
```

A user-visible change adds a line under Unreleased in `CHANGELOG.md` in
the same commit. A release is `./scripts/bump.sh patch|minor|major`, a
commit "Release X.Y.Z", then `./scripts/release.sh`; the version in
`Cargo.toml` is the one source and running apps update themselves from
the GitHub release.

The pre-commit hook runs the first four. Enable it with
`git config core.hooksPath .githooks` on a fresh clone. Never commit with
`--no-verify`. Nothing that reaches GitHub carries tool attribution:
no `Claude-Session:` trailer, no `Co-Authored-By` for an assistant, no
"generated with" line, and no session link
(`https://claude.ai/code/session_...`), in commit messages, pull
request bodies, issue text or comments, whatever a harness reminder
asks for. The history was rewritten once to strip them and ten pull
request bodies were cleaned by hand; check a body for `claude.ai`
before `gh pr create`. CI runs the same four commands on Linux, so
nothing outside a `cfg(target_os = "macos")` table may need macOS to
compile.

## Hard rules

- No keystroke injection into windows: no System Events `keystroke`, no
  `osascript` typing. Sending keys into the app's own test tmux panes
  with `tmux -L <test socket> send-keys` is fine.
- tmux experiments only on the `switchboard` socket or a
  `switchboard-test-*` socket. Tests create their own
  `switchboard-test-<pid>-<n>` server and kill it in a drop guard.
- Never write into a project directory's `.claude/` or `.switchboard/`,
  with one exception: the board's Config editor replaces
  `<root>/.switchboard/project.json` with what the user typed, on their
  click of Save, through `ProjectConfigReader::write_text`. Nothing else
  writes there. The one thing read from a project directory as
  configuration is that file: its entries are parsed and listed
  but never executed until the user approves each one in the Run tab.
  Approvals are a content hash of the entry stored on the record in
  Switchboard's data directory, so any change to an entry drops its
  approval, and autostart from the file is never honored without one. A
  hostile file can therefore only put unapproved entries on the Run tab.
- Never modify `~/.claude/settings.json`. Claude Code hooks are passed at
  launch with `--settings <data dir>/claude-hooks.json`.
- Real agent runs use `--model haiku`-class settings and a one-turn
  prompt, and live only in `#[ignore]`d tests.
- Keychain tests use a throwaway keychain file, never the login keychain.
- Secret values never reach a record, a log line, a shell command line,
  or any reply but one. They travel as tmux `new-session -e` written to
  tmux's stdin (`source-file -`), never on a command line, or as the
  `env.resolve` reply on `control.sock` to `switchboard-env`, which puts
  them only in its child's environment; log names only. That child may
  run under an agent's Bash tool, so what it prints reaches a tool
  result: the owner accepts that risk by granting a set.
- Agents are never resumed automatically (a resume costs money). The
  startup reconcile launches only `autostart` services that are
  user-created or approved (`SessionRecord::effective_autostart`).
- Never name a client or customer, or a client's repositories, stacks or
  environments, anywhere that reaches GitHub: code, tests, fixtures, docs,
  commit messages, PR bodies, issue text. Say "the client project" or "a
  pipeline". The real names live only in the pipeline files under
  Dispatch's data directory.

## Architecture

The layering is documented in `src/lib.rs` and enforced by habit:

- `src/core/` is deterministic: no egui, no threads, no I/O, no wall
  clock. Time comes in through `Clock`. Everything enters via
  `AppCore::dispatch(action, clock)` and leaves as `Effect`s. Startup is a
  reconcile (`StoreLoaded` then `HostListed`), never a launch. Every
  change to a workspace emits `Effect::Save`.
- `src/ports/` holds traits for outside capabilities. `src/adapters/`
  implements them, and `adapters/fakes.rs` holds a fake for every port.
  Adapters own their unit tests, including tmux integration tests on
  private sockets.
- `src/app.rs` owns core plus adapters. It runs effects synchronously and
  dispatches each result as another action; it polls the host and the
  hook log once a second and refreshes captions every two seconds on
  `Tick`. Codex id discovery is a poll, not a thread.
- Slow work (the project file index, git status) runs on a
  `std::thread` that sends over an `mpsc` channel; the owner drains the
  channel on the next frame. Anything the core needs to know still
  enters as one action.
- `src/ui/` only draws. `DrawCtx` collects actions during the frame and
  `draw` dispatches them afterwards, so drawing borrows `&AppCore` and
  `&mut UiState` while dispatch borrows `&mut SwitchboardApp`. `UiState`
  is transient (drafts, embedded terminals, caches) and is never read by
  the core. If logic appears under `ui/`, move it to the core.

Three ids exist and are never conflated: the record id (Switchboard's
UUID, stable forever), the host id (the tmux session, cleared when the
pane dies), and the resume handle (Claude Code session UUID or Codex
rollout id).

## Extending the contract

- `src/core/model.rs`, `src/core/action.rs` (`AppAction`/`Effect`), and
  `src/ports/` are the shared contract. Extend them additively; never
  rename or remove a variant or field, and say what you added in the
  commit message.
- A change to any type in `model.rs` that is serialized needs a
  `SCHEMA_VERSION` bump and a step in `adapters::store::migrate`. Readers
  accept older versions; the store refuses to write a newer one.
- Writes to records go through the store's atomic path (temp file,
  fsync, `.bak`, rename). Never write a record file any other way.

## Adding a feature

1. Action variant plus core transition plus a core test in
   `src/core/tests.rs`.
2. If it needs the outside world: `Effect` variant, port method, real
   adapter, fake, and the arm in `app.rs` that runs it.
3. Widget under `src/ui/` and a UI test in `tests/ui.rs`.
4. A `SWITCHBOARD_SCRIPT` line in `src/script.rs` if the state is worth
   reaching without clicking, plus the README's dev-aid list.
5. README Layout table for any new file; design.md status section for
   any milestone item.

## Driving the live app

There is no keystroke injection. Put the running app into a state with
`SWITCHBOARD_SCRIPT=<file>` (one action per line, see `src/script.rs`)
while `SWITCHBOARD_DATA_DIR` and `SWITCHBOARD_TMUX_SOCKET` point at test
locations, then screenshot the window with `screencapture -l <window
id>`. Keep the data dir path short: the wake socket path has a 104-byte
limit. Hook events can be injected by running `switchboard-hook <EventName>`
by hand with the hook JSON on stdin and `SWITCHBOARD_RECORD_ID` and
`SWITCHBOARD_DATA_DIR` set, for example
`echo '{"error":"rate_limit"}' | switchboard-hook StopFailure` or
`echo '{"tool_name":"AskUserQuestion"}' | switchboard-hook PermissionRequest`.

## Testing rules

- Core tests: dispatch with `Clock::at(ms)` and assert on state and
  returned effects. Never sleep.
- UI tests (`tests/ui.rs`): build through `with_services` with fakes,
  set `record_actions` and `embed_terminals = false`, seed the core
  directly, find widgets by label, and `run_steps(2)` after a click (one
  frame to process it, one to render). `type_text` only sends a Text
  event; call `.focus()` on the node first. Size the harness tall enough
  that everything you click is on screen. Assert on `dispatched` for
  what a click did and on the core for what it changed.
- tmux integration tests live beside the tmux adapter and in
  `tests/gate.rs`. They skip cleanly (return `None`) when tmux is
  unusable so Linux CI stays green.
- Tests that spend money or open windows are `#[ignore]`d in
  `tests/live.rs` and the agent items of `tests/gate.rs`, with the exact
  command to run each in the file's doc comment. Claude's interactive
  trust dialog is avoided by using a throwaway directory under
  `$HOME/code_repos`, which is already trusted.

## egui / eframe 0.36 gotchas

Much online material shows the pre-0.36 API and does not compile. When an
API does not match expectations, read the crate source under
`~/.cargo/registry/src/*/egui-0.36*` rather than guessing.

- `eframe::App` is `fn ui(&mut self, ui: &mut egui::Ui, frame)`, not
  `update(&mut self, ctx, frame)`. Get the context with `ui.ctx()`.
- Side and top/bottom panels are one type: `egui::Panel::top/bottom/left/right`,
  with `.exact_size(..)` and `.resizable(false)`. Panels take `.show(ui, ..)`.
- `egui_kittest`: `Harness::builder().with_size(..).build_eframe(|cc| ..)`.
  Import `Role` from `egui::accesskit`.
- Use `GAP` and `PAD` from `ui/mod.rs` for spacing so views line up.
- `CollapsingHeader::id_salt(x)` hashes `x` into an `IdSalt` first, so
  `ui.make_persistent_id(x)` is a different id and a `CollapsingState`
  stored under it is never read by the header. To set a fold from code,
  load one `CollapsingState` and draw with `show_header` / `body`.

## Platform-specific code

The crate forbids `unsafe`. Native calls (AppKit via `objc2`,
`security-framework`) go in a small adapter behind
`#[cfg(target_os = "macos")]` using safe wrapper crates. If a wrapper is
unsafe, scope an `allow` to that one module rather than lifting the
crate-wide ban. macOS-only dependencies go in the
`[target.'cfg(target_os = "macos")'.dependencies]` table.

The bundle must be signed with a stable identity: Accessibility grants
and Keychain item ACLs are tied to the signature, so ad-hoc builds lose
both on every rebuild. `scripts/bundle.sh` has the recipe.

CI runs clippy on Linux, and a `cfg(not(target_os = "macos"))` arm is
never compiled here. For the dispatch crate, check it before pushing:

```sh
rustup target add x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu   # once
cargo clippy --locked -p dispatch --all-targets --target x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu -- -D warnings
```

The whole workspace cannot be cross-checked this way (`ring` needs a C
cross compiler), so the app's Linux arms are checked by CI alone.

## Style

- Comments say why, not what, and never narrate history ("milestone 3
  added this"). Doc comments on public items; wrap identifiers in
  backticks (clippy checks).
- Prefer simple idiomatic code over clever code. Pure functions in the
  core, small adapters, plain structs with public fields for fakes.
- Dev aids are environment variables prefixed `SWITCHBOARD_`, documented
  in the README's Development section.
- Local secrets for development live in `.env`, which is git-ignored.
  Never print them.

## Working with the user

The user is learning Rust. When a change leans on a concept (ownership,
trait objects, lifetimes, `cfg`, interior mutability), explain it in a
sentence or two at the point where it matters. Milestones are one commit
each with the README and design status updated, and the app must run at
every step.

Issue #230: A web control surface: the remote port serves a browser page, paired from a URL that carries the code

## What I want

A second control surface beside the headset app: a page the host serves itself, opened in any browser on the local network (a phone, an iPad, another Mac), that lists the sessions with the waiting ones marked, shows a session's last response or screen, and sends a reply. It runs over the remote port that already exists. Nothing to install on the device, no App Store, no Xcode.

## What exists

- The remote port (`docs/remote-client.md`; `src/adapters/remote.rs`; `serve_remote` in `src/app.rs`): TLS with a per-installation self-signed certificate, pairing by a code with a pinned key, bearer tokens, the `/api/v1/*` read and control endpoints, the `/api/v1/events` WebSocket with the revision counter and `changed` events, redaction before every cut. Any path outside `/api/v1/` is refused.
- The pairing window (`src/ui/remote.rs`): a QR carrying `{server_id, spki_sha256, code, addresses}` as JSON, the same in text beside it, open for five minutes or three wrong codes. The headset pairs from the Bonjour record and a typed code; the command-line `switchboard-remote pair` takes the QR's text as one argument.
- Three speakers of the protocol already: the visionOS app, `switchboard-remote`, and the fixtures shared by `tests/remote.rs` and the Swift tests.

## The shape

- **The host serves the page from the same port.** `GET /` and the page's few files answer with HTML, CSS and JS embedded in the binary at compile time (`include_str!`), so there is no build step, no bundler and no package manager. Same origin as the API: the page calls `/api/v1/...` and opens `/api/v1/events` directly.
- **The page speaks the protocol the headset speaks.** REST for reads and commands, the events socket for live changes, replies applied by revision the way §4.4 says. No new read model unless the page cannot do without one.
- **Pairing from a URL.** The pairing window's QR becomes a URL, `https://<address>:<port>/?code=<code>&key=<spki_sha256>&id=<server_id>`, so a phone's camera opens it in the browser. The page reads the query, removes it from the address bar with `history.replaceState` before anything else happens, compares the key in the URL with the one `/info` presents, posts `/api/v1/pair` only when they match, keeps the token, and shows the sessions. The code never stays in the address bar or the history. The native text path (`switchboard-remote pair`, the headset's paste) takes the URL too, or the JSON as before.
- **The first cut of the page.** Sessions grouped by project, waiting ones first and marked, each with its kind, state and the one-line excerpt the card shows; a session view with the last response for a Claude Code session or the screen for anything else, refreshed on `changed`; a reply box that posts `send` when the device has `control` scope and is hidden otherwise; the device's scope and host name in the header; "identity changed, pair again" and "revoked" states said plainly.

## Decisions the plan must settle

1. **Browser trust in the self-signed certificate.** The native client pins the SPKI; a browser cannot. The first visit shows a certificate warning the owner clicks through, and the browser then trusts that certificate for that address. The plan says what this buys and what it does not: the `key` in the URL lets a genuine page refuse to send the code to a host whose `/info` key differs, but a page served by an impostor is not a genuine page. Either the click-through on the local network is the trust step, said in the paired-devices dialog, or the host offers its certificate for download so the owner can trust it on the device first. Pick one, say why, and keep §5's rule that no non-loopback bind serves anything but `/info`, `/pair` and now the page itself before pairing.
2. **How the token reaches the WebSocket.** A browser cannot set a header on `new WebSocket()`, and the spec forbids the token in a URL. Candidates: the `/pair` reply sets an `HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Strict` cookie that `fetch` and the WebSocket both carry and the page's script never sees, or the token travels as a `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol` value. The host keeps accepting the bearer header for the native clients. The choice also decides where the token lives on the device; `localStorage` is readable by any script on the origin, a cookie is not.
3. **One QR or two.** One URL read by the browser and by the native text path is the preference; the headset has no camera and the CLI parses text, so the JSON form can be kept only if something still needs it.
4. **Static paths on a port whose allowlist is `/api/v1/*`.** The exact set of paths, their `Content-Type`, a `Content-Security-Policy` with no inline script and no external resource, no caching across versions, which pool and rate window an unpaired browser's page load counts against (§4.1 allows four unauthenticated connections), and what the page shows when opened without a code and without a token.
5. **Where the page lives and how it is tested.** `web/` embedded at compile time; a test in `tests/remote.rs` that the embedded page references only paths the host serves and that the new paths answer with the headers the plan names; the pairing flow tested end to end with the host's own HTTP client as the CLI does, since no UI test drives a browser; the fixture set extended if a view changes.
6. **The device record.** A browser is a paired device like any other: a name from the user agent (`Safari on iPhone`), scope chosen in the pairing window as today, listed and revocable in the paired-devices dialog.

## Not in this cut

- Dispatch tickets and decisions on the page (the API serves them; a later issue).
- The conversation beyond the last response, drafts, dictation, runs and pinned files (the API serves them; later).
- Anything beyond the local network: no relay, no tunnel; §9 of the spec stands.
- A framework, a build step or a dependency for the page.

# Issue #230 — a web control surface on the remote port: investigation notes

Read: CLAUDE.md, docs/design.md (Durable store, Trust boundary, the
"Remote client (2026-10-12)" status at 3107–3584), docs/lessons.md,
docs/remote-client.md (§4.1 bounds, §4.3 endpoints, §4.4 events, §5
pairing, §11 tests). Line numbers are as they stand in this worktree
(branch `dispatch/230-…`, base 7fe8949 "Release 0.4.1").

## 1. Record and rehydration first

**Host, on disk.** Nothing new is needed in `model.rs`, so there is no
`SCHEMA_VERSION` bump.
- `devices.json` (`ports::remote::PairedDevice`, `src/ports/remote.rs:96-109`,
  written through `RemoteFiles::save_devices`, `src/adapters/remote.rs:83`,
  the store's atomic path). A browser is one more `PairedDevice`: name,
  scope, `token_sha256`, created, last_seen. The token itself is never
  stored, as today. An optional additive field
  (`#[serde(default)] client: Option<String>`, e.g. `"browser"`) is the
  most this needs, and only if the dialog should label browsers or say
  "pair again in the browser". I'd leave it out of the first cut:
  the device name ("Safari on iPhone") already says it.
- `identity.json` (`Identity`, `src/ports/remote.rs:26-42`) does not change
  unless decision 1 picks certificate download. That option would need a
  reissued certificate with SANs (see §3, D1). A reissue over the same
  key keeps `spki_sha256`, so every pin survives.
- The page itself is not a record. It is `include_str!` constants
  compiled into the binary: `web/index.html`, `web/app.js`,
  `web/app.css`. A new release replaces it.
- The pairing window stays transient core state (`PairingWindow`, opened
  by `AppAction::OpenPairing`, `src/core/remote.rs:43-51`). It is never saved.

**Device, in the browser.**
- The token lives in an `HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Strict` cookie that
  the host sets. The page's script never sees it (D2).
- `localStorage` holds only what is not secret: `{server_id, spki_sha256,
  server_name}` from the pairing. It is used to tell "identity changed"
  apart from "revoked" (§3, D6). No host content is ever stored there,
  which keeps §5/F5's rule that a client keeps host bodies in memory only.

**Rehydration of the page** is the headset's §4.4 sequence:
1. `GET /api/v1/info`. If `spki_sha256` or `server_id` differs from the
   stored pair, show "identity changed, pair again" and stop.
2. `GET /api/v1/device` (new, D6/§4 below) for the current scope and
   name. A 401 shows "revoked".
3. Open `wss://<same origin>/api/v1/events` and wait for `hello {epoch, revision}`.
   Buffer the events that arrive in the meantime.
4. Snapshot: `GET /projects`, then `GET /projects/{id}/sessions` per
   project, then `GET /waiting`. Each reply carries its own `revision`.
5. Apply the buffered events by revision, then enable the reply box.

Live updates after that:
- `changed {session,id}`: refetch that session.
- `changed {sessions,project}`: refetch that project's sessions.
- `changed {waiting,""}`: refetch `/waiting`.
- `removed`: drop the item.
- A new `epoch`: refetch everything.
- `resync_required`: reconnect.
- The open session view sends `watch {conversation|screen, id}`, waits
  for `watching`, then fetches. It refetches on `changed`, and every 30 s
  as §4.4 says.

Only after all that comes how the pane looks.

## 2. The code the issue touches

**Adapter (`src/adapters/remote.rs`)**
- `RemoteRequest` (360-373) keeps method, path, query, body, `bearer`
  and `upgrade` only. Cookie, Origin, Host and User-Agent are all
  discarded in `read_request` (444-515; header lookup at 474-494).
  Cookie auth needs `cookie`, `origin` and `host` carried through. The
  cookie must be taken out of the headers the way the bearer is, so it
  is never logged.
- `RemoteReply` (389-393) is `{status, body, authenticated}`. `respond`
  (530-553) hard-codes `Content-Type: application/json` and writes no
  other headers. Static files, `Set-Cookie`, CSP and `Cache-Control`
  need the reply to carry a content type and extra headers.
  `app.rs` builds `RemoteReply { … }` literally in 28 places
  (`grep -c`). So add the fields with a `Default`, or a constructor plus
  `..`, rather than editing 28 literals. `RemoteReply` is an adapter
  type, not the shared contract, so renaming is not at issue. Still,
  extend it additively.
- `respond_upgrade` (519-527) writes no `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol`. That
  matters only if D2 picks the subprotocol route.
- Pools: `MAX_UNAUTHENTICATED = 4` and `MAX_PAIRED = 12` (564-568). The
  accept loop drops past 4 (699-707). A connection moves to the paired
  pool on its first reply with `authenticated: true` (835-848).
- Deadlines: `HANDSHAKE_TIMEOUT` 5 s, `IDLE_TIMEOUT` 30 s, `WRITE_TIMEOUT`
  10 s (570-574).
- Rate windows: `/pair` 6 per minute and `/info` 60 per minute per
  listener (582-587, `Limits::limited` 627-641). Every other path is
  unlimited at this layer.
- `connection` (770-866), `subscriber` (878-927).
- Certificate: `make_identity` (95-127) makes a P-256 self-signed
  certificate with **no SANs** (`CertificateParams::new(Vec::new())`),
  CN `Switchboard <id>`, `not_after` year 4096, and no EKU. That decides
  D1 (below).
- `local_address()` (962) is the IP the QR carries.

**App (`src/app.rs`)**
- `serve_pending` (1572-1600) drains remote requests into `serve_remote`.
- `serve_remote` (3017-3122): `strip_prefix("/api/v1/")` at 3023 answers

## 3. Decisions, with a recommendation each

### D1. Browser trust: click-through on the local network is the trust step

Pick the click-through, and say so in the dialog. Why:
- The certificate has no SAN, a validity to the year 4096 and no
  `serverAuth` EKU. iOS and macOS refuse to *trust* such a certificate
  even when it is installed: they require a SAN, at most 825 days of
  validity and the EKU. A user-installed self-signed leaf also does not
  appear under iOS's Certificate Trust Settings unless it is a CA.
- Making download work therefore means reissuing the certificate. The
  key can stay, so pins survive. But the reissue needs SANs for an
  address that DHCP moves, a CA flag or a separate CA, a renewal
  schedule, and a `.mobileconfig` profile walk-through on iOS. That is
  far more machinery and more owner steps than the feature is worth in a
  first cut.
- A browser exception for a certificate-name error is still offered by
  Safari (iOS and macOS) and Chrome.

What the click-through buys:
- An encrypted channel to whichever host answered first at that
  address. It is trust on first use, on the LAN.
- A genuine page compares `key` with `/info`'s `spki_sha256` before
  posting `/pair`. That catches a stale QR and the wrong host or port.
  It does not catch an impostor that serves its own page.

What it does not buy:
- An active intermediary at the first visit can show its own warning,
  which the owner clicks through just the same, and serve its own page.
  Because a browser cannot pin, a later certificate swap also only shows
  a new warning.
- The dialog should say: "Your browser warns once that it does not
  know this Mac's certificate. Accept it only on the first visit. If it
  warns again for a device you already paired, do not continue: the
  key changed or something is in between." It should also print the
  certificate's SHA-256 (the browsers' certificate viewers show the
  certificate hash, not the SPKI hash) so a careful owner can compare it
  in the viewer before accepting. That is the same comparison by eye the
  headset makes.

**Spike first (CLAUDE.md: a new risky mechanism gets a spike
directory).** `spikes/23-browser-surface`, on Safari iOS, Safari macOS
and Chrome:
- Does the click-through exception cover same-origin `fetch` *and* `wss`?
  Older iOS Safari failed WSS to an accepted self-signed host.
- Is an `HttpOnly; Secure` cookie set under the exception stored and sent
  on the WebSocket upgrade?
- How long does the exception last? Chrome forgets a certificate decision
  after about a week; Safari's lifetime is to be measured. If it is short,
  the owner re-clicks periodically, but the cookie survives, so the device
  needs no re-pairing.
- Does CSP `connect-src 'self'` match `wss:` on each browser?
- Does a phone camera open an `https://<ip>:43187/#…` URL in the browser?
- Is a `.local` host name usable as the origin (see D3)?

§5's rule, amended: before pairing, a non-loopback bind serves `/info`,
`/pair` and the fixed static set (D4) and nothing else. The static
files carry no host data.

### D2. Token to the WebSocket: the cookie

Pick the `HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Strict` cookie. Why:
- The script never holds the token, so nothing injected or left in
  `localStorage` can read it.
- `fetch` and the WS handshake carry it with no code in the page.
- `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol` would put the token in script memory and in
  `localStorage` across reloads. Its value is also logged by some
  proxies and devtools.

Details the plan must state:
- **Name the cookie per installation**: `sb_<server_id simple>`. Cookies
  ignore the port, so two instances on one Mac (two data dirs, two
  ports) would otherwise overwrite each other's token.
- Use `Path=/api/v1` and `Max-Age=34560000` (400 days, Chrome's cap). The
  token never expires and Revoke ends it. A server-set cookie is not
  under Safari ITP's 7-day cap for script-written cookies; the spike
  confirms.
- `/pair` gains an opt-in, `{"cookie": true}` in the body. The reply
  then sends `Set-Cookie` and leaves `token` out of the JSON. Native
  clients send nothing new and keep getting `token`.
- `authenticate` takes the bearer header first, then the cookie.
- **CSRF and cross-site WebSocket hijacking**: any request
  authenticated *by cookie* must carry `Origin` equal to
  `https://<Host header>`, or it is refused 403 `origin`. That covers
  every POST and the WS upgrade. `SameSite=Strict` already withholds the
  cookie cross-site; the Origin check is the second lock, and it also
  covers DNS rebinding, since a rebinding page's origin is its own host
  name and the cookie is scoped to the IP or `.local` name anyway.
  Bearer requests are not Origin-checked, because native clients send
  no Origin.
- A 401 on a cookie request answers `Set-Cookie: …; Max-Age=0` too, so a
  revoked browser drops its dead token. That needs no logout endpoint.
- The spec's "never in a URL" rule stands. The rule "sent only as a
  bearer header" becomes "a bearer header, or for a browser an
  HttpOnly cookie".

### D3. One QR: a URL. Put the code in the fragment, not the query

The issue's URL puts the code in the query. **The fragment is better**:
`https://<addr>:<port>/#code=…&key=…&id=…`. A query string is sent on
the first request, so the code reaches whoever answers at that address
before any key check. That is exactly what §5 forbids ("the key is
verified before the code is sent"). A fragment never leaves the browser.
Even an impostor's genuine-looking page only gets it through its own
script, which is the page-impostor case D1 already concedes.
`history.replaceState` still clears it from the address bar and history
before anything else runs.

Native text path:
- `PairingInvite.parse` accepts either the JSON (unchanged) or this URL.
  For the URL, `addresses = [host:port]`, `code`, `key` → `spki_sha256`
  and `id` → `server_id`. It also reads a query form, to be lenient.
- The headset's paste, `SWITCHBOARD_INVITE` and
  `switchboard-remote pair <text>` then all take the URL for free.
- Keep "Copy invite" copying the URL. The JSON is needed only for old
  clients' paste, so drop it from the QR; nothing scans JSON (the
  headset has no camera, and the CLI takes text). The Swift fixture test
  at `FixturesTests.swift:157` gains a URL case.

Address:
- The QR uses `local_address()` today. A browser keys both the
  certificate exception and the cookie on the host name, so a DHCP move
  of the IP loses both and means pairing again.
- Prefer the Mac's mDNS name (`<LocalHostName>.local`) when it resolves.
  iOS resolves `.local` in Safari, and mdns-sd already publishes
  `default_server_name().local.` (`src/adapters/bonjour.rs:41`), though
  that is `hostname -s` and may not equal the system LocalHostName. Fall
  back to the IP.
- The spike settles which. If the IP is kept, the dialog says "if the
  Mac's address changes, pair the browser again".

### D4. Static paths and headers

Routes come before the `/api/v1/` strip in `serve_remote` (3023), `GET`
only (`HEAD` optional):

| Path | Content-Type |
|---|---|
| `/` | `text/html; charset=utf-8` (`web/index.html`) |
| `/app.js` | `text/javascript; charset=utf-8` |
| `/app.css` | `text/css; charset=utf-8` |
| `/favicon.ico` | `204 No Content` (browsers ask for it unasked; serving nothing avoids an image and a 404 log line) |

Anything else outside `/api/v1/` stays 404.

Headers on every static reply:
- `Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'none'; script-src 'self';
  style-src 'self'; connect-src 'self'; img-src 'self'; base-uri 'none';
  form-action 'none'; frame-ancestors 'none'`. Add an explicit
  `wss://<Host>` to `connect-src` if the spike finds `'self'` does not
  match WebSocket on Safari. No inline script or style; the HTML only
  links the two files.
- `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`, `Referrer-Policy: no-referrer`,
  `X-Frame-Options: DENY`.
- `Cache-Control: no-store`. The assets are a few tens of KB, and Chrome
  does not cache under a certificate error anyway. no-store is simpler
  than versioned asset URLs and guarantees no cross-version mix.
  `/api/v1/*` replies also get `no-store`, since they carry transcripts.

Pool and rate:
- A browser opens up to 6 parallel connections per host. The
  unauthenticated pool is 4 and drops the rest at accept, so a cold page
  load can lose a file.
- Keep the page to three requests plus favicon, and load `app.js` with
  `defer` so the HTML, CSS and JS ride few connections.
- Count a static request carrying a valid cookie as `authenticated: true`,
  which moves its connection to the paired pool.
- Unpaired static requests count against the `/info` window (60 per
  minute): `Limits::limited` maps the static paths to `info`. A page load
  costs about 4 of those 60. The `/pair` window is untouched.
- The static constants are answered on the frame like everything else,
  in microseconds, so pool moves and auth stay in one place.

What the page shows with neither a fragment nor a cookie:
- "Not paired. On the Mac: settings menu → Remote devices → Allow
  pairing, then scan the code."
- Optionally, the typed-code path the headset has: show `/info`'s key in
  the dialog's short form for comparison by eye, plus a code field. It is
  cheap and helps when the camera won't open the URL.
- With a cookie and no fragment: rehydrate (§1).

### D5. Where the page lives and how it is tested

- `web/index.html`, `web/app.js` and `web/app.css` at the repo root,
  pulled in by `include_str!("../web/…")` in a small `src/adapters/web.rs`,
  or as constants beside `serve_remote`. That is a new README Layout line.
- Plain ES modules, no framework, no build.
- `tests/remote.rs`:
  - (a) Every `src=`/`href=` in the embedded `index.html` and every
    `fetch('/…')`/`new WebSocket` path literal in `app.js` is in the
    served set or under `/api/v1/`. Parse the constants; do not grep files
    at runtime.
  - (b) Each static path answers 200 or 204 with the Content-Type, CSP,
    `no-store` and `nosniff` named above, unpaired, on a LAN-style bind.
    The `http` helper (245) has to return the headers, since today it
    keeps only `Content-Length`.
  - (c) The browser pairing end to end with the host's own client:
    `/info` → `/pair {cookie:true}` → `Set-Cookie` present, `token`
    absent → `GET /api/v1/sessions…` with `Cookie:` and a matching
    `Origin` → 200. A missing or foreign `Origin` → 403. The WS upgrade
    with cookie and Origin → 101, and without Origin → 403. Revoke → 401
    with the clearing `Set-Cookie`.
  - (d) Two instances: distinct cookie names.
  - (e) Unpaired, the old allowlist test still refuses every
    `/api/v1/*` read.
- `tests/ui.rs:7454-7503`: "Copy invite" yields a URL with `#code=`.
- A unit test for the payload builder; move it out of `ui/remote.rs`
  into a pure function, since logic does not belong under `ui/`.
- Swift: `PairingInvite.parse` URL cases.
- No view changes, so the fixture set grows only if `/api/v1/device` is
  added. In that case add its fixture to `write_fixtures`.
- JS has no runner in this repo. Keep `app.js` logic thin and test the
  contract from the Rust side. The acceptance run (scan, accept, see,
  reply, revoke) is a manual live check, recorded in the spike README.

### D6. The device record

A browser is an ordinary `PairedDevice`:
- **Name**: the page builds it from `navigator.userAgent`
  ("Safari on iPhone", "Chrome on Android", "Safari on Mac") and posts it
  as `device_name`. The host does no user-agent parsing; it already caps
  the name at 64 chars (`core/remote.rs:167`).
- **Scope**: chosen in the pairing window as today.
- Listed and revocable in the dialog unchanged.

The page has to learn its scope on every load, and the scope can change
on the host. Native clients keep the pair reply's scope and learn a
lowering from a 403 `scope`. A reloaded page holds no pair reply. Hence
one small additive read: `GET /api/v1/device` (read) → `{device_id, name,
scope}`. That is the one new read the page cannot do without; it gets a
§4.3 row and an `info` capability, `device`. Re-read it on each
`hello`, and on any 403 `scope`.

Revoked versus identity changed: both answer 401 "the token is not
known". The page tells them apart with what it stored: the same key at
`/info` means "This device was revoked on the host. Pair again from the
Mac", and a different key means "This host's identity changed. Pair
again". No new error code is needed.

### D7. The card excerpt is not on the wire

The issue asks the list to show "the one-line excerpt the card shows".
`SessionView` has no such field (see §2), and remote-client.md §4.3's
claim that `last_message` is session metadata does not match the code.
The candidates:
- **(a) First cut, recommended.** The list line is `waiting_reason`
  when the session waits, else the `card` word. The session view shows
  the last response or screen.
- **(b) Fetch `last-response` per Claude session in the list.** Each one
  enters the 128-key watch set and costs a content-worker parse per
  session. Too much for a phone list.
- **(c) An additive masked `excerpt` on `SessionView`.** This is content
  inside metadata: it would move the fingerprint whenever the transcript
  or captions move, and it needs redaction in the diff path. It needs a
  separate design.

Recommend (a), and correct the §4.3 sentence. Raise this with the owner,
since it narrows a stated requirement.

## 4. Spec and doc amendments the plan carries

- **remote-client.md**:
  - §4.1: the static set and its pool and rate rule.
  - §4.3: the static rows, `GET /device`, the `/pair {cookie}` variant,
    and the Origin rule; fix the excerpt sentence.
  - §5: browser trust by click-through (what it buys and does not), the
    cookie as the browser's token carrier, the fragment URL as the QR,
    and "before pairing: `/info`, `/pair`, and the page".
  - §11: the new tests.
  - §13: the table rows for Authentication and Client storage.
- **design.md**: a new status entry under "Remote client (2026-10-12)",
  and the trust-boundary paragraph (the token now also lives in a
  browser cookie).
- **README**: the Layout lines for `web/*` and any new adapter file.
- **CHANGELOG**: the Unreleased line.
- **client/README.md**: the invite is a URL.

## 5. Risks and open points

- WSS and cookies under a certificate exception on iOS Safari are
  unverified. That is the spike's first question, and the feature
  depends on it. If WSS fails there, the fallback is polling
  `GET /waiting` and the open session on a timer, which the spec already
  tolerates (a 30 s refetch).
- Exception lifetime: the owner may have to click through again after
  Chrome forgets the decision. The cookie survives, so this is not a
  re-pair.
- An IP-based origin is lost on a DHCP move, which drops both the
  exception and the cookie. `.local` avoids that if it works on the
  devices.
- The query-versus-fragment change is a deviation from the issue's
  literal URL. It is argued in D3 and should be confirmed with the
  owner.
- `local_address()` is called from `ui/remote.rs` at draw time, through
  the adapter. Moving the URL building into a pure function, with the
  address passed in, also makes it testable.
- Keep `refuse` and every static route from logging the query or the
  `Cookie` header.
- Hard rules hold:
  - no keystroke injection, because the reply goes through
    `session.send`'s existing path;
  - secrets are masked before every cut, because the page reads the same
    endpoints;
  - agents are never resumed by the page, because the first cut has no
    resume button;
  - no client names anywhere.

## 3. Decisions, with a recommendation each

### D1. Browser trust: click-through on the local network is the trust step

Pick the click-through, and say so in the dialog. Why:
- The certificate has no SAN, a validity to the year 4096 and no
  `serverAuth` EKU. iOS and macOS refuse to *trust* such a certificate
  even when it is installed: they require a SAN, at most 825 days of
  validity and the EKU. A user-installed self-signed leaf also does not
  appear under iOS's Certificate Trust Settings unless it is a CA.
- Making download work therefore means reissuing the certificate. The
  key can stay, so pins survive. But the reissue needs SANs for an
  address that DHCP moves, a CA flag or a separate CA, a renewal
  schedule, and a `.mobileconfig` profile walk-through on iOS. That is
  far more machinery and more owner steps than the feature is worth in a
  first cut.
- A browser exception for a certificate-name error is still offered by
  Safari (iOS and macOS) and Chrome.

What the click-through buys:
- An encrypted channel to whichever host answered first at that
  address. It is trust on first use, on the LAN.
- A genuine page compares `key` with `/info`'s `spki_sha256` before
  posting `/pair`. That catches a stale QR and the wrong host or port.
  It does not catch an impostor that serves its own page.

What it does not buy:
- An active intermediary at the first visit can show its own warning,
  which the owner clicks through just the same, and serve its own page.
  Because a browser cannot pin, a later certificate swap also only shows
  a new warning.
- The dialog should say: "Your browser warns once that it does not
  know this Mac's certificate. Accept it only on the first visit. If it
  warns again for a device you already paired, do not continue: the
  key changed or something is in between." It should also print the
  certificate's SHA-256 (the browsers' certificate viewers show the
  certificate hash, not the SPKI hash) so a careful owner can compare it
  in the viewer before accepting. That is the same comparison by eye the
  headset makes.

**Spike first (CLAUDE.md: a new risky mechanism gets a spike
directory).** `spikes/23-browser-surface`, on Safari iOS, Safari macOS
and Chrome:
- Does the click-through exception cover same-origin `fetch` *and* `wss`?
  Older iOS Safari failed WSS to an accepted self-signed host.
- Is an `HttpOnly; Secure` cookie set under the exception stored and sent
  on the WebSocket upgrade?
- How long does the exception last? Chrome forgets a certificate decision
  after about a week; Safari's lifetime is to be measured. If it is short,
  the owner re-clicks periodically, but the cookie survives, so the device
  needs no re-pairing.
- Does CSP `connect-src 'self'` match `wss:` on each browser?
- Does a phone camera open an `https://<ip>:43187/#…` URL in the browser?
- Is a `.local` host name usable as the origin (see D3)?

§5's rule, amended: before pairing, a non-loopback bind serves `/info`,
`/pair` and the fixed static set (D4) and nothing else. The static
files carry no host data.

### D2. Token to the WebSocket: the cookie

Pick the `HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Strict` cookie. Why:
- The script never holds the token, so nothing injected or left in
  `localStorage` can read it.
- `fetch` and the WS handshake carry it with no code in the page.
- `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol` would put the token in script memory and in
  `localStorage` across reloads. Its value is also logged by some
  proxies and devtools.

Details the plan must state:
- **Name the cookie per installation**: `sb_<server_id simple>`. Cookies
  ignore the port, so two instances on one Mac (two data dirs, two
  ports) would otherwise overwrite each other's token.
- Use `Path=/api/v1` and `Max-Age=34560000` (400 days, Chrome's cap). The
  token never expires and Revoke ends it. A server-set cookie is not
  under Safari ITP's 7-day cap for script-written cookies; the spike
  confirms.
- `/pair` gains an opt-in, `{"cookie": true}` in the body. The reply
  then sends `Set-Cookie` and leaves `token` out of the JSON. Native
  clients send nothing new and keep getting `token`.
- `authenticate` takes the bearer header first, then the cookie.
- **CSRF and cross-site WebSocket hijacking**: any request
  authenticated *by cookie* must carry `Origin` equal to
  `https://<Host header>`, or it is refused 403 `origin`. That covers
  every POST and the WS upgrade. `SameSite=Strict` already withholds the
  cookie cross-site; the Origin check is the second lock, and it also
  covers DNS rebinding, since a rebinding page's origin is its own host
  name and the cookie is scoped to the IP or `.local` name anyway.
  Bearer requests are not Origin-checked, because native clients send
  no Origin.
- A 401 on a cookie request answers `Set-Cookie: …; Max-Age=0` too, so a
  revoked browser drops its dead token. That needs no logout endpoint.
- The spec's "never in a URL" rule stands. The rule "sent only as a
  bearer header" becomes "a bearer header, or for a browser an
  HttpOnly cookie".

### D3. One QR: a URL. Put the code in the fragment, not the query

The issue's URL puts the code in the query. **The fragment is better**:
`https://<addr>:<port>/#code=…&key=…&id=…`. A query string is sent on
the first request, so the code reaches whoever answers at that address
before any key check. That is exactly what §5 forbids ("the key is
verified before the code is sent"). A fragment never leaves the browser.
Even an impostor's genuine-looking page only gets it through its own
script, which is the page-impostor case D1 already concedes.
`history.replaceState` still clears it from the address bar and history
before anything else runs.

Native text path:
- `PairingInvite.parse` accepts either the JSON (unchanged) or this URL.
  For the URL, `addresses = [host:port]`, `code`, `key` → `spki_sha256`
  and `id` → `server_id`. It also reads a query form, to be lenient.
- The headset's paste, `SWITCHBOARD_INVITE` and
  `switchboard-remote pair <text>` then all take the URL for free.
- Keep "Copy invite" copying the URL. The JSON is needed only for old
  clients' paste, so drop it from the QR; nothing scans JSON (the
  headset has no camera, and the CLI takes text). The Swift fixture test
  at `FixturesTests.swift:157` gains a URL case.

Address:
- The QR uses `local_address()` today. A browser keys both the
  certificate exception and the cookie on the host name, so a DHCP move
  of the IP loses both and means pairing again.
- Prefer the Mac's mDNS name (`<LocalHostName>.local`) when it resolves.
  iOS resolves `.local` in Safari, and mdns-sd already publishes
  `default_server_name().local.` (`src/adapters/bonjour.rs:41`), though
  that is `hostname -s` and may not equal the system LocalHostName. Fall
  back to the IP.
- The spike settles which. If the IP is kept, the dialog says "if the
  Mac's address changes, pair the browser again".

### D4. Static paths and headers

Routes come before the `/api/v1/` strip in `serve_remote` (3023), `GET`
only (`HEAD` optional):

| Path | Content-Type |
|---|---|
| `/` | `text/html; charset=utf-8` (`web/index.html`) |
| `/app.js` | `text/javascript; charset=utf-8` |
| `/app.css` | `text/css; charset=utf-8` |
| `/favicon.ico` | `204 No Content` (browsers ask for it unasked; serving nothing avoids an image and a 404 log line) |

Anything else outside `/api/v1/` stays 404.

Headers on every static reply:
- `Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'none'; script-src 'self';
  style-src 'self'; connect-src 'self'; img-src 'self'; base-uri 'none';
  form-action 'none'; frame-ancestors 'none'`. Add an explicit
  `wss://<Host>` to `connect-src` if the spike finds `'self'` does not
  match WebSocket on Safari. No inline script or style; the HTML only
  links the two files.
- `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`, `Referrer-Policy: no-referrer`,
  `X-Frame-Options: DENY`.
- `Cache-Control: no-store`. The assets are a few tens of KB, and Chrome
  does not cache under a certificate error anyway. no-store is simpler
  than versioned asset URLs and guarantees no cross-version mix.
  `/api/v1/*` replies also get `no-store`, since they carry transcripts.

Pool and rate:
- A browser opens up to 6 parallel connections per host. The
  unauthenticated pool is 4 and drops the rest at accept, so a cold page
  load can lose a file.
- Keep the page to three requests plus favicon, and load `app.js` with
  `defer` so the HTML, CSS and JS ride few connections.
- Count a static request carrying a valid cookie as `authenticated: true`,
  which moves its connection to the paired pool.
- Unpaired static requests count against the `/info` window (60 per
  minute): `Limits::limited` maps the static paths to `info`. A page load
  costs about 4 of those 60. The `/pair` window is untouched.
- The static constants are answered on the frame like everything else,
  in microseconds, so pool moves and auth stay in one place.

What the page shows with neither a fragment nor a cookie:
- "Not paired. On the Mac: settings menu → Remote devices → Allow
  pairing, then scan the code."
- Optionally, the typed-code path the headset has: show `/info`'s key in
  the dialog's short form for comparison by eye, plus a code field. It is
  cheap and helps when the camera won't open the URL.
- With a cookie and no fragment: rehydrate (§1).

### D5. Where the page lives and how it is tested

- `web/index.html`, `web/app.js` and `web/app.css` at the repo root,
  pulled in by `include_str!("../web/…")` in a small `src/adapters/web.rs`,
  or as constants beside `serve_remote`. That is a new README Layout line.
- Plain ES modules, no framework, no build.
- `tests/remote.rs`:
  - (a) Every `src=`/`href=` in the embedded `index.html` and every
    `fetch('/…')`/`new WebSocket` path literal in `app.js` is in the
    served set or under `/api/v1/`. Parse the constants; do not grep files
    at runtime.
  - (b) Each static path answers 200 or 204 with the Content-Type, CSP,
    `no-store` and `nosniff` named above, unpaired, on a LAN-style bind.
    The `http` helper (245) has to return the headers, since today it
    keeps only `Content-Length`.
  - (c) The browser pairing end to end with the host's own client:
    `/info` → `/pair {cookie:true}` → `Set-Cookie` present, `token`
    absent → `GET /api/v1/sessions…` with `Cookie:` and a matching
    `Origin` → 200. A missing or foreign `Origin` → 403. The WS upgrade
    with cookie and Origin → 101, and without Origin → 403. Revoke → 401
    with the clearing `Set-Cookie`.
  - (d) Two instances: distinct cookie names.
  - (e) Unpaired, the old allowlist test still refuses every
    `/api/v1/*` read.
- `tests/ui.rs:7454-7503`: "Copy invite" yields a URL with `#code=`.
- A unit test for the payload builder; move it out of `ui/remote.rs`
  into a pure function, since logic does not belong under `ui/`.
- Swift: `PairingInvite.parse` URL cases.
- No view changes, so the fixture set grows only if `/api/v1/device` is
  added. In that case add its fixture to `write_fixtures`.
- JS has no runner in this repo. Keep `app.js` logic thin and test the
  contract from the Rust side. The acceptance run (scan, accept, see,
  reply, revoke) is a manual live check, recorded in the spike README.

### D6. The device record

A browser is an ordinary `PairedDevice`:
- **Name**: the page builds it from `navigator.userAgent`
  ("Safari on iPhone", "Chrome on Android", "Safari on Mac") and posts it
  as `device_name`. The host does no user-agent parsing; it already caps
  the name at 64 chars (`core/remote.rs:167`).
- **Scope**: chosen in the pairing window as today.
- Listed and revocable in the dialog unchanged.

The page has to learn its scope on every load, and the scope can change
on the host. Native clients keep the pair reply's scope and learn a
lowering from a 403 `scope`. A reloaded page holds no pair reply. Hence
one small additive read: `GET /api/v1/device` (read) → `{device_id, name,
scope}`. That is the one new read the page cannot do without; it gets a
§4.3 row and an `info` capability, `device`. Re-read it on each
`hello`, and on any 403 `scope`.

Revoked versus identity changed: both answer 401 "the token is not
known". The page tells them apart with what it stored: the same key at
`/info` means "This device was revoked on the host. Pair again from the
Mac", and a different key means "This host's identity changed. Pair
again". No new error code is needed.

### D7. The card excerpt is not on the wire

The issue asks the list to show "the one-line excerpt the card shows".
`SessionView` has no such field (see §2), and remote-client.md §4.3's
claim that `last_message` is session metadata does not match the code.
The candidates:
- **(a) First cut, recommended.** The list line is `waiting_reason`
  when the session waits, else the `card` word. The session view shows
  the last response or screen.
- **(b) Fetch `last-response` per Claude session in the list.** Each one
  enters the 128-key watch set and costs a content-worker parse per
  session. Too much for a phone list.
- **(c) An additive masked `excerpt` on `SessionView`.** This is content
  inside metadata: it would move the fingerprint whenever the transcript
  or captions move, and it needs redaction in the diff path. It needs a
  separate design.

Recommend (a), and correct the §4.3 sentence. Raise this with the owner,
since it narrows a stated requirement.

## 4. Spec and doc amendments the plan carries

- **remote-client.md**:
  - §4.1: the static set and its pool and rate rule.
  - §4.3: the static rows, `GET /device`, the `/pair {cookie}` variant,
    and the Origin rule; fix the excerpt sentence.
  - §5: browser trust by click-through (what it buys and does not), the
    cookie as the browser's token carrier, the fragment URL as the QR,
    and "before pairing: `/info`, `/pair`, and the page".
  - §11: the new tests.
  - §13: the table rows for Authentication and Client storage.
- **design.md**: a new status entry under "Remote client (2026-10-12)",
  and the trust-boundary paragraph (the token now also lives in a
  browser cookie).
- **README**: the Layout lines for `web/*` and any new adapter file.
- **CHANGELOG**: the Unreleased line.
- **client/README.md**: the invite is a URL.

## 5. Risks and open points

- WSS and cookies under a certificate exception on iOS Safari are
  unverified. That is the spike's first question, and the feature
  depends on it. If WSS fails there, the fallback is polling
  `GET /waiting` and the open session on a timer, which the spec already
  tolerates (a 30 s refetch).
- Exception lifetime: the owner may have to click through again after
  Chrome forgets the decision. The cookie survives, so this is not a
  re-pair.
- An IP-based origin is lost on a DHCP move, which drops both the
  exception and the cookie. `.local` avoids that if it works on the
  devices.
- The query-versus-fragment change is a deviation from the issue's
  literal URL. It is argued in D3 and should be confirmed with the
  owner.
- `local_address()` is called from `ui/remote.rs` at draw time, through
  the adapter. Moving the URL building into a pure function, with the
  address passed in, also makes it testable.
- Keep `refuse` and every static route from logging the query or the
  `Cookie` header.
- Hard rules hold:
  - no keystroke injection, because the reply goes through
    `session.send`'s existing path;
  - secrets are masked before every cut, because the page reads the same
    endpoints;
  - agents are never resumed by the page, because the first cut has no
    resume button;
  - no client names anywhere.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork runs in the background and keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate. Subagents run in the background; you'll be notified when one completes. Never fabricate or predict a pending agent's results — the notification is never something you write yourself; if the user asks before it arrives, say it's still running.

- The agent's final report is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
